title: March 4, 2026 – Customer Spotlight: Midland Fire Department Enhances Radiation Detection with SAM 950
body:
The Midland Fire Department has strengthened its emergency response capabilities by upgrading its radiation detection technology, giving firefighters faster, more accurate insight during hazardous-material incidents and other emergencies.

With the support of grant funding, the department added the Berkeley Nucleonics SAM 950 handheld radiation detection system. This SAM 950 is designed specifically for first responders, nuclear field analysts, and specialized military and security teams.

According to Lt. Tyler Alden, the new system has become a valuable operational asset.

“It is an asset. It makes our department quicker,” Alden said. “It makes our response to radiation faster.”

Bringing Radiation Detection into the Modern Era

The department received the SAM 950 in January and now shares it across stations among trained personnel. While radiation monitoring has long been part of Midland Fire’s mission, the new technology represents a major step forward.

“This equipment brings our radiation detection from the 1960s into modern day,” Alden noted.

With real-time analysis and advanced identification capabilities, responders can quickly determine what type of radiation is present and how to proceed safely.

“It tells us what kind of radiation it is,” Alden explained. “It tells us if it was medical radiation or ill intent.”

Advanced Capabilities in a Handheld Platform

The SAM 950 combines multiple critical tools into one portable system, including:

  • Radiation survey meter
  • Spectral analysis
  • Secondary screening
  • Isotope identification and confirmation
  • Source location features

These capabilities support hazmat response, medical and industrial monitoring, event security, and port and border enforcement.

By consolidating these functions into a single device, Midland firefighters can respond more efficiently and with greater situational awareness.

Rapid Training and Deployment

Firefighters trained on the SAM 950 were able to learn the system in just one day, allowing the department to deploy it quickly across multiple stations.

This rapid adoption ensures more personnel are prepared to operate the equipment when needed—improving readiness and response times.

Commitment to Safety and Innovation

By investing in modern radiation detection technology, the Midland Fire Department continues to demonstrate its commitment to public safety and operational excellence. The SAM 950 enhances the department’s ability to protect first responders and the community while staying ahead of evolving threats.

Adapted from: “Midland Fire enhances radiation detection” by Tereasa Nims, Midland Daily News, May 13, 2022.

title: November 18, 2025 – Skip the Chamber: How the SPECTRAN V6 Enables Real-Time EMI Testing Anywhere
body:
The SPECTRAN V6 Real-Time Spectrum Analyzer is transforming how engineering teams approach EMI pre-compliance testing. Conventional methodologies typically depend on slow swept analyzers and access to a shielded chamber, which can create project delays and make it difficult to identify transient issues. The V6 architecture introduces ultra-fast scanning, real-time visibility, and intelligent noise-removal tools that help engineers find problems much earlier in the design cycle.

With sweep rates up to 3 THz/s, the system can scan very wide frequency ranges in only milliseconds. Sweeping a 1 GHz band with a 120 kHz RBW achieves roughly a 1.7 ms probability of intercept, allowing emissions and short bursts to surface immediately instead of being missed between sweeps. This delivers a much clearer picture of switching noise, digital interference, and other intermittent effects.

A major advantage is the ability to run meaningful EMI pre-compliance without a shielded room. Using the Spectral Background Mask block, the analyzer records all ambient RF activity and builds a mask to remove environmental noise. This often drops the ambient spectrum by nearly 20 dB and produces a clean spectrum for DUT measurements, even in noisy environments. Tests can be done at the bench, in a lab, or even in a simple tent setup, which offers far more flexibility than the traditional chamber-only approach.

The V6 also provides a 30 ns probability of intercept in real-time mode, making it possible to capture very short events. Transients from power supplies, processors, and mixed-signal systems appear instantly. With a frequency range from 9 kHz to 140 GHz, the platform supports nearly every modern EMI and wireless application.

The software includes standard EN, CISPR, and FCC limit lines, and additional limits—such as FMC or custom profiles—can be added quickly using the built-in power limit editor. Users can also record and save spectra for documentation, before/after comparisons, reference measurements, or long-term troubleshooting.

A typical EMI setup includes the V6 analyzer, HyperLOG and BicoLOG antennas, a pre-amplifier, an OCXO timebase, and the Spectral Background Mask option, along with a high-performance PC using USB 3.2 and a Ryzen 8-core processor with 64 GB RAM. Optional shielding cubes, tripods, and compass modules help build a more complete workflow. The SPECTRAN V6 provides a much faster and more flexible method for EMI pre-compliance, allowing engineers to troubleshoot quickly, shorten redesign cycles, and work without the limitations of a dedicated chamber.

title: June 13, 2025 – Why the Model 686 is the Go-To AWG for Semiconductor Testing
body:
When it comes to testing today’s advanced semiconductor devices, precision and speed are non-negotiable. Test engineers are constantly challenged to replicate high-speed signals with fidelity and control. That’s where the Model 686 Arbitrary Waveform Generator (AWG) from Berkeley Nucleonics comes in. Offering an unmatched blend of speed, resolution, and versatility, it delivers exactly what’s needed for modern semiconductor validation. Let’s take a closer look at what makes this AWG a standout in its class.

Exceptional Speed and Resolution

The Model 686 delivers a real-time sampling rate of 20 GS/s and up to 6.5 GHz sine output, all while maintaining a true 14-bit resolution. That level of performance means you can emulate the kind of signals seen in PCIe Gen3, USB 3.0, and other high-speed digital systems. It’s not just fast—it’s clean, giving you low-distortion waveforms that reveal how your devices behave under real-world conditions.

Sharp Transitions and Signal Strengths

Semiconductor testing often requires precise edge transitions and varied voltage levels. With a rise time of just 50 ps and output voltages reaching 5 Vpp, the Model 686 enables both. Whether you’re testing a fast-switching digital circuit or an analog front end, this AWG gives you the signal sharpness and strength to do it properly.

Synchronized Analog and Digital Outputs

Each unit can output up to four analog channels along with 32 digital lines, all running in tight sync. This is especially useful for mixed-signal testing—like running a baseband signal while toggling control lines or injecting parallel data. Everything lines up in time, so your test results are as reliable as your setup.

Room for Complexity

Test scenarios aren’t always simple. Fortunately, the Model 686 gives you 9 GSamples of memory per channel, letting you load extensive waveform data without breaking a sweat. Complex multi-step test sequences, real-world signal captures, or stress patterns—this AWG handles them with ease.

Built to Scale

As your test requirements grow, so can the Model 686. Connect up to four units via its internal synchronization bus and you’re working with 16 analog and 128 digital outputs—without losing timing accuracy. Great for parallel testing or large-scale IC evaluation.

User-Friendly from the Start

The included Simple Rider software is just what it sounds like—simple. It’s touchscreen-ready and designed to make waveform creation and device control intuitive. Whether you’re setting up pulse trains or working on custom digital patterns, the interface won’t slow you down.

Purpose-Built for Semiconductor Work

From high-speed interface simulation to power device characterization, the Model 686 is well suited for semiconductor labs. You can generate PRBS data streams, control voltage ramps, or emulate noisy environments—all with one box. It’s built to handle whatever modern test benches demand.

A Tool That Grows with You

Beyond semiconductors, the Model 686 is also a staple in photonics, aerospace, and RF labs. That versatility makes it a solid investment—not just for today’s needs, but tomorrow’s challenges too.

Final Thoughts

The Model 686 isn’t just another AWG. It’s a tool that’s been engineered to keep up with how fast the semiconductor industry is evolving. For test engineers who need dependable, high-performance signal generation, this instrument checks every box.

title: May 21, 2025 – Model 686 Application Note: AWGs for QKD & Quantum Sensors
body:
Introduction

In our digital age, sensitive information from financial transactions to classified government data flows through networks at an unprecedented rate. However, conventional encryption methods that rely on mathematical algorithms face an existential threat from quantum computers.

Quantum computers could easily crack these encryption codes when they become powerful enough. This encapsulates the urgency to develop quantum-resistant encryption methods. QKD stands at the forefront of this endeavor.

The laws of quantum mechanics are used not only to protect our communications and data, but also to understand the world around us at an unprecedented level of detail. Light, temperature, pressure, heat, and other things imperceptible to more traditional sensors can be measured by quantum sensors. Quantum sensors depend on the constants of nature, so their reliability never degrades; they are self-calibrating and their measurements don’t drift over time like traditional sensors do.

High performance AWGs like the Model 686 are becoming extremely popular in designing and developing these emerging breakthrough technologies.

QKD: Quantum Key Distribution

Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is a secure communication method for exchanging encryption keys known only between shared parties. It uses properties found in quantum physics to exchange cryptographic keys in a way that is provable and guarantees security. QKD enables two parties to produce and share a key used to encrypt and decrypt messages.

Key distribution on a conventional scale relies on public key ciphers that use complicated mathematical calculations requiring a prohibitive amount of processing power to break. The viability of public key ciphers, however, faces several issues, and quantum computing will render most of today’s public key encryption strategies unsafe.

QKD is different from conventional key distribution because it uses a quantum system that relies on basic and fundamental laws of nature to protect the data, rather than relying on mathematics.

QKD works by transmitting many light particles, or photons, over fiber optic cables between parties. Each photon has a random quantum state, and collectively the photons sent make up a stream of ones and zeros—qubits, the equivalent of bits in a binary system. When a photon reaches its receiving end it travels through a beam splitter, which forces the photon to randomly take one path or another into a photon collector.

The receiver responds to the original sender with data regarding the sequence of the photons sent, which the sender then compares with what was originally transmitted. Photons in the wrong beam collector are discarded; what’s left is a specific sequence of bits that can be used as a key to encrypt data. Any errors and data leakage are removed during a phase of error correction and other post-processing steps.

Photons are polarized when they oscillate in only one direction, and polarizing filters let us filter for that. Quantum mechanics has made it possible to send single photons; if the receiver holds a filter the same way as the sender’s polarization, the light passes through, and if crosswise, no photon passes—meaning each photon can be measured only once.

Quantum Key Exchange

The two parties compare notes publicly on how photons were polarized and how filters were held, discarding the cases where one used a diagonal filter and the other vertical or transverse, and building their key from what remains.

If an eavesdropper tries to read along a photon with a polarization filter, they must send a new photon onward afterward, without knowing whether they held their filter correctly. Because photons cannot be copied and can only be measured once, an eavesdropper must guess often, introducing detectable errors. Comparing individual digits of the key before use reveals whether anyone has been listening, which is what makes the quantum encryption approach effectively unbreakable.

Types of QKD

There are many types of QKD, but two main categories are prepare-and-measure protocols and entanglement-based protocols.

Prepare-and-measure protocols focus on measuring unknown quantum states and can detect eavesdropping and estimate how much data may have been intercepted.

Entanglement-based protocols rely on quantum states in which two objects are linked, so that measuring one affects the other; if an eavesdropper accesses a previously trusted node and changes something, the other parties will know.

It is difficult to implement an ideal infrastructure for QKD. It is perfectly secure in theory, but in practice, imperfections in tools such as single photon detectors create security vulnerabilities, so security analysis remains important.

Modern fiber optic cables are typically limited in how far they can carry a photon, often to around 100 km, though some groups have extended this considerably—for example, the University of Geneva and Corning Inc. constructed a system capable of carrying a photon 307 km under ideal conditions.

Another challenge of QKD is that it relies on having a classically authenticated channel of communication already established. As quantum computers become more common, however, the risk that an attacker could crack current encryption methods rises, making QKD more relevant.

QKD Attack Methods

Even though QKD is secure in theory, imperfect implementations have the potential to compromise security. For example, the phase remapping attack takes advantage of the fact that a device must allow signals to enter and exit, creating a backdoor used against methods common in many commercial QKD systems.

Another attack method is the photon number splitting attack: in practice more than one photon is often sent at a time, and extra photons could be intercepted without either party knowing. Decoy state QKD, an improvement to the BB84 protocol, mixes decoy signals in with the intended signal so both parties can detect an eavesdropper.

QKD Implementation Methods

There are two approaches to implementing QKD: discrete variable QKD (DV-QKD), which relies on single photons with encoded random data, and continuous variable QKD (CV-QKD), which plays on the wave nature of light with information encoded in the quadrature of its electromagnetic fields, read out with coherent homodyne or heterodyne detection.

Different modulation solutions exist for the transmitter side (Alice) and optical hybrid demodulators for the receiver side (Bob). One of the most technologically advanced intensity modulators is the Exail NIR-MX800, whose LiNbO3 modulation offers high bandwidth, high contrast, and ease of use.

The Model 686 and Model 685 series can drive these Electro-Optic Modulators directly to generate very short optical pulses. Their ability to generate pulses with 50 ps rise/fall time, 100 ps pulse width, and 5 Vpp amplitude allows driving the EOM without an external amplifier. Using, for example, Exail’s NIR-MX800 with the BNC Model 686, very short optical pulse widths from 100 ps can be achieved at 850 nm, 1310 nm, and 1550 nm—without an external amplifier between the AWG and the modulator.

Quantum Sensors

Quantum sensors allow us to understand the world around us at an unprecedented level of detail, improving the accuracy of how we measure, navigate, study, explore, see, and interact with the world by sensing changes in motion and electric and magnetic fields, with data collected at the atomic level.

This allows quantum sensors to make technological devices exponentially more accurate, thorough, efficient, and productive, and to be less vulnerable to signal jamming and other electromagnetic interference than conventional light- and sound-based sensors. Applications include more accurate geolocation than GPS allows, more detailed medical diagnostic imaging, safer autonomous navigation, more accurate guidance systems, mapping of underground environments, and more sensitive detection of gravitational and tectonic changes.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging

MRI quantum sensors have been around for decades: MRI machines use quantum sensors and manipulate a quantum property called spin within the body’s atoms, measuring the response of those spins to a magnetic field and transforming it into an image.

Atomic clocks are another kind of quantum sensor, in use since the 1950s to keep time in GPS satellites and define the SI unit of a second. Newer technologies make additional quantum sensors and applications possible, including nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers fabricated within diamonds.

An NV center forms when a carbon atom in a diamond’s crystal lattice is replaced by a nitrogen atom next to a vacant lattice site. The resulting defect has its own quantum spin, effectively a tiny magnet, that is sensitive enough to detect magnetic field changes tens of millions of times smaller than the strength of Earth’s magnetic field—even in the presence of that background field.

The spin can be altered by electromagnetic radiation or a magnetic field, and the NV center is also photoluminescent: lit with green light, it emits a red glow whose brightness depends on the spin state. By monitoring changes in that brightness under microwave or magnetic field excitation, researchers can measure the strength of a magnetic field—a technique called optically detected magnetic resonance.

The BNC Model 686 has been used to control the experimental pulse sequences used to manipulate single tin vacancy centers in diamond, generating narrow electrical square pulses with amplitude up to 5 Vpp to drive an electro-optical amplitude modulator and produce short laser pulses with a close to Gaussian shape and a full-width-half-maximum as narrow as 130 ps.

The Model 686 can also drive an electro-optical phase modulator to generate frequency sidebands up to about 7 GHz, enabling two optical transitions to be driven with phase-stable laser fields, while its digital output channels control acousto-optical amplitude modulators or generate trigger pulses for timing experimental sequences.

title: April 25, 2025 – The PVX-2506: It’s a Voltage Source, It’s a Current Source, It’s Everything!
body:
Hi there, my name is Cameron Simmons and I am an applications engineer here at Berkeley Nucleonics. Today I am going to do a video about one of our lesser known products—the PVX-2506. It is a hybrid voltage current pulser. We refer to it as a precision voltage pulser, and it’s got a lot of cool features that may help your application.

The PVX-2506 is what we refer to as a precision pulse generator, because we tune the overshoot and undershoot so that it never exceeds the pulse top and bottom voltage. This can be really good for semiconductor material testing because you know your material is never exposed to a voltage higher than required for your testing, and you can get great data on it. The unit can do 50 volts at 10 amps, which is extremely high for a voltage pulser of this type, so the PVX-2506 can be used to test a lot of high voltage and high current semiconductor materials.

Another great feature is that the 2506 accepts a high voltage power supply and a lower voltage power supply, so you can actually float it up to ten volts. This can be really good if that’s the voltage you want tested at, or if you just want a less noisy signal moving above ground—that will take out some of the noise and help you get cleaner data.

The cable included with the 2506 is heavy duty, with gold pads and very low inductance. It can take a lot of voltage while remaining very low inductance, so you’re not going to get any added overshoot and zero ringing, which makes this overall a very good cable for this application.

An interesting feature of the PVX-2506 is a utility section that will help you invert and copy your trigger signal, so you can take one trigger in from your source and put it into the RF logic input. You’ll get a TTL copy of that signal and an inverted TTL version of it, and either can trigger RF as well—so you can put a sinusoidal waveform in and it will create a square trigger signal. This makes testing and collecting data easier without having to have an external box that does this.

On the oscilloscope, the output of the voltage pulser is a nice clean 30 volt pulse into a 5 ohm load—no aberrations, no overshoots, very square, low noise. Zooming in on the rising edge shows the overshoot tuning at work: the top never exceeds the actual pulse top, meaning the rising and falling edges are finely tuned. The falling edge is the same—it never exceeds ground, and you can get some very clean data with this.

The output of the PVX-2506 is floating and has two voltage inputs, so you can bias it up just to reject noise if that’s what your experiment calls for—for example, running at about 30 volts to ground and then engaging the second power supply to bias it up about 10 volts further. That’s the PVX-2506.

title: April 16, 2025 – A Competitive High Power Current Source: The PCX-7500-EX
body:
What makes a high power current source stand out amongst its competitors? Precision pulse control, exceptional ease of use from setup through operation, and complete system integration. These are the factors that define the PCX-7500-EX as a notable option for a high power current source.

The PCX-7500-EX is most suitable for driving laser diodes, bars, and arrays. It has voltage drops up to 110V, output power up to 1000W, an adjustable pulse width between 4 µs and 5,000 µs, and a settable output current ranging from 10A to 450A.

The unit uses an external DC power supply to source the laser diode forward voltage, which has a host of advantages—perhaps most notably the ability to source a variety of laser diodes at full output from a single device up to a 110 volt diode array, simply by matching the DC supply to the diode’s forward voltage. That makes it a versatile tool to have in the arsenal.

A good product also needs a well designed chassis: the PCX-7500-EX has conveniently located front panel BNC connectors that allow it to be externally triggered and synchronized for specialized interconnected equipment applications. The input impedance of the trigger is selectable to either 50Ω or 10,000Ω, and the synchronization output pulse is synchronized to the leading edge of the output current pulse and is active with internal or external trigger.

title: April 4, 2025 – The PVX-4141 at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams
body:
Introduction

It is a great treat to learn about the ways in which our equipment from Berkeley Nucleonics has improved applications, driven solutions, and provided answers for research teams at some of the most decorated institutions across the world. Most recently, we’ve touched base with a researcher at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams (FRIB) following their purchase and use of the PVX-4141 bipolar pulse generator, involved in the design and testing of a fast machine protection system and chopper monitor system.

In this operation, the PVX-4141 is tested for use in a linear accelerator to verify that the bipolar pulse generator works fast enough for the intensive operations at FRIB—and it does. Here is a quick synopsis of what this type of rigorous unit testing entails, from its beginning concepts to its conclusion.

Design

The design of the system is relatively common. The IOC/OPI is the user interface: the user can set threshold values, different beam modes, and verify that each element of the system is working as intended.

The chopper monitor system takes analog information from the PVX-4141 and other parts of the accelerator systems, digitizes it, and uses an FPGA to compensate for small changes in the beam in real time. This is done by modulating the frequency and width of the gate signal controlling the PVX-4141’s pulse width and repetition rate—in other words, the PVX voltage monitor and current monitor provide the data used to maintain stable operation.

Pulse Checker

The signal from the PVX-4141 is not static: the width and frequency are “ramped,” or slowly increased in a linear fashion, in different phases. The pulse checker monitors the ramp rate and ensures it is behaving correctly.

Voltage and Current Monitor

The voltage monitor (VMON) and current monitor (IMON) feed into the ADC and are processed by the FPGA, which performs the math on the received digital data. To read the very fast current pulses, the IMON signal is integrated with a capacitor during the rising edge, reset before the falling edge, then reset again afterward before the next pulse—creating a clear, readable signal for the FPGA to measure the current flowing in and out of the plates that accelerate the particle beam.

Test in Beam Line

In the validation results, a green status line moves from “beam started” to “beam on.” A red fault line rising from zero causes the green line to indicate the beam stopping, then off. This test verified that the beam auto-shutdown works, and that the time it takes the PVX-4141 to react to the error is short enough to stop any damage from taking place.

Conclusion

This exercise highlights the PVX-4141’s aptitude for integration in scientific testing and research. This model, as well as the entire PVX line, is already set up so that useful information for automation and real-time feedback is available—making it an ideal candidate for use in large, complex systems where every aspect must be measured and monitored.

title: March 18, 2025 – Multi- and Single- Channel Analyzer Options
body:
What is a Multichannel Analyzer?

Multichannel Analyzers (MCAs) constitute essential components in spectroscopy systems. An MCA comprises two primary elements: the analog-to-digital converter (ADC) and computer-addressable memory. Berkeley Nucleonics provides multiple MCA options, enabling users to configure systems aligned with their specific application requirements.

The Model 970: Portable Multichannel Analyzer

This MCA distinguishes itself through flexible architecture accommodating diverse applications—functioning as a process monitor, standalone laboratory instrument, or integrated system component for analysis. The unit offers modular assembly, compact packaging, and intuitive software, supporting applications across both spectroscopy and spectrometry domains.

TOPAZ-Pico

Advanced digital electronics underpin the TOPAZ-pico design, establishing it as a fully digital, compact, standalone advanced MCA. The unit incorporates a miniaturized high-voltage power supply optimized for low consumption, delivering 0 to 1,500 volts in 4096 steps to power PMT tubes, with two data acquisition modes supporting operational flexibility.

PHA acquisition mode offers spectral memory size options of 256, 512, 1024, 2048, and 4096 channels; coarse gain with amplification factors of 1, 2, 4, and 8; fine gain adjustment from 1 to 2 in 1/4096 increments; and upper and lower level discriminator settings configured in channels.

MCS acquisition mode offers the same spectral memory size options, dwell time adjustment from 0.1 seconds to count-forever, and simplified setup via regions of interest or nuclide information.

bPAD Compact Single Channel Analyzer

The bPAD is a microprocessor-based Single Channel Analyzer (SCA) integrating preamplifier, amplifier, and discriminator within a compact photomultiplier tube base. Particularly suited for count rate monitoring within specific energy regions of interest, this unit incorporates a programmable high-voltage power supply with output voltage settable from 0 to 1500 volts. Microprocessor control enables straightforward operation, with USB-based configuration via provided software, and two operational modes: integral mode (counts above a single energy threshold) and differential mode (counts within a defined energy window).

bPAD+ is an enhanced variant incorporating an additional analog pulse output connectable to external MCAs for monitoring purposes, maintaining full digital architecture and its associated advantages.

bPAD+VR is an advanced bPAD+ version permitting analog output configuration as either pulse signal transmission or variable voltage proportional to discriminated count rate—valuable for flow count rate instruments and HPLC systems.

bPAD/VR/HPLC is functionally equivalent to bPAD+VR, with multi-parameter setup software specifically configured for HPLC applications.

bGamma Software Package for Gamma Spectroscopy Analysis

The bGamma software package furnishes comprehensive tools for detailed gamma-ray spectrum analysis and radionuclide quantification. This general-purpose application connects and controls hardware for data acquisition, imports spectra from alternate file formats, executes energy, shape, and efficiency calibration, fits experimental data to mathematical models (including background subtraction and peak interference correction), calculates radionuclide activity levels, performs automatic peak searching and classification, conducts region-of-interest analysis, and performs nuclide identification with separation from potential spectrum artifacts.

title: March 7, 2025 – Big Physics: Model 765 Pulse Generator Application Note
body:
Photomultiplier Characterization and Calibration

In big physics experiments, the use of photomultipliers is fundamental and common. The photomultiplier converts an electrical charge for an acquisition system, allowing photons to be detected. The emission of photons can be correlated to a specific phenomenon studied by physicists, such as the Cherenkov effect.

During the design and production of a photomultiplier, it is necessary to characterize and calibrate it using a laser or an LED diode. The light source must be driven by a preassigned signal with a fixed width and sequence. Using the Model 765 pulse generator from Berkeley Nucleonics, it is now easier than ever to generate a pulse with various widths, periods, and amplitudes. Setup is intuitive and easy: setting a single pulse puts the instrument waiting for an external trigger-in, or it can generate pulses continuously.

Klystron Control and Synchronization

A klystron is a specialized linear-beam vacuum tube used in multiple applications—for example, in the colliders used for big physics experiments, where it generates the particles that will collide. Much like driving a light source to characterize a photomultiplier, it is necessary to generate a signal to drive the klystron.

That signal can be generated by a complex system based on a logic port or an FPGA, but the design and development of such systems is lengthy and restrictive; any sudden need to change the timing means changing the schematic or the FPGA code. The Model 765 offers an off-the-shelf solution to control and modify klystrons, with a touchscreen display that lets users simply enable signal parameters.

When driving a klystron, the user can also synchronize multiple units to the Model 765. With up to 4 independent channels, the user can set independent synchronization signals with specific delays from the trigger signal—allowing multiple klystrons to be synchronized while accounting for and compensating the delay between the different driving chains.

Data Acquisition and FPGA Testing

In big physics experiments, detectors observe different physical phenomena, but the acquisition chain that collects and stores real-time data is equally important. The read-out chain is based on a hierarchic tree structure where the lowest level, near the detectors, converts digital pulses using a communication protocol to deliver information to the next level.

Usually the lowest level is composed of an FPGA system that collects the digital pulses of multiple detectors, creating a data packet to deliver to the next level via an optical link. During development of such a system, engineers usually do not have access to detectors or the entire collider, making it necessary to find easier ways to simulate the pulses detectors would generate.

Using the BNC Model 765 pulse generator, it is possible to test the response of an FPGA system and ensure its timing and synchronization settings hold—for example, inspecting what happens if channels have skew, or testing the receipt of multiple pulses for glitches. The Model 765 offers up to 4 channels, each able to deliver single, double, triple, or quadruple pulses, with each pulse independently set for period, width, and delay relative to the trigger-in signal.

title: February 25, 2025 – Lessons from the Lab: PVX Bias
body:
This technical piece, authored by BNC electrical engineer Cameron Simmons, is excerpted from a video demonstration and addresses modifying a PVX-4151 high voltage pulse generator to enable 1,000-volt output biasing.

Device Overview

The PVX-4151 functions as a bipolar pulse generator with dual high voltage inputs for positive and negative polarity. The power supply voltages must remain within a 1,500-volt differential, though they can be asymmetrically distributed around zero—such as -500V to 1000V, -750V to 750V, or 0V to 1,500V configurations.

Design Challenge

The modification allows the device to pulse between 1,000 and 2,500 volts while respecting the differential limit. This capability serves applications like parallel-plate time-of-flight mass spectrometers, where both plates must operate at elevated voltages, with one plate pulsing slightly higher to achieve a specific particle velocity.

Technical Solution

The approach requires two positive polarity high voltage power supplies, with the lower 5 kV unit acting as bias voltage. The main complication is that most high voltage power supplies cannot independently regulate same-polarity outputs from separate sources—the higher voltage supply typically pulls the lower voltage toward its potential. A shunt resistor from the bias supply to ground maintains independent voltage regulation.

The shunt resistance follows R = Vbias / Ips, and power dissipation in capacitive loads follows P = C×V²×F. For the specific implementation, with a 50 pF capacitor connected via 2 feet of RG58 cable plus the PVX-4151’s internal 200 pF capacitance, the engineer selected a 62 megohm resistor built from soldered 10 megohm, 1-watt resistors with spade connectors and kapton tape insulation for arc prevention.

Final Outcome

The modification delivers a 1,500-volt pulse spanning from 1,000 to 2,500 volts output. Customers interested in the technique can contact Berkeley Nucleonics or visit the PVX-4151 product page for implementation assistance.

title: February 13, 2025 – Creating Tail Pulses Using the Sequencer on an Arbitrary Waveform Generator
body:
I’m Edgar, one of the engineers here at Berkeley Nucleonics, and I’m going to go over how to use our Model 670C—or any of our arbitrary waveform generators—to generate a sequence of pulses. In this case, I’m going to mimic the pulse that would come out of our BH-1, since that unit is no longer manufactured, by duplicating that signal using an arbitrary waveform generator.

Starting from the 670C’s default settings outputting a standard sine wave, I add a second entry to the sequencer—the sequencer can hold up to several thousand waveforms, depending on the application—and build a tail pulse using the exponential rise and exponential decay waveforms built into the 670C and the other Model 600 series ARBs, like the 675 and 685.

To get the required timing, I go into advanced settings and the trigger menu to set the period of the interval—in this case one millisecond, roughly one kilohertz. In Edit Entry, I set the jump sequence: sequence one to sequence two and back, set to timer, so it waits one millisecond before resetting to output the next waveform. With that in place, the unit outputs the exponential rise and exponential decay at roughly one kilohertz.

From there I set the lengths and durations of the exponential rise and exponential decay depending on the rise time and fall time I want—it’s not exact, but for example a 450 nanosecond duration and interpolation/decimation setting gets roughly a 50 nanosecond rise time, and a similar approach on the decay side—say 500 microseconds to get roughly a 100 microsecond fall time. Because this is an arbitrary waveform generator, I’m working more in terms of how many points and how long a waveform runs, rather than frequency directly, as I would with a dedicated pulse or delay generator.

That wraps up one of many ways an AWG can generate a tail pulse—the right approach generally depends on the goal and application. If you have any type of waveform you need to see, need to mimic outdated BNC equipment, or need the function of equipment no longer in production, reach out by phone or email; we can help determine whether your desired application is feasible on our arbitrary waveform generators or other products we make. Arbitrary Waveform Generators are extremely versatile, and we’re excited to push the boundaries of our units alongside your work.

title: February 7, 2025 – Non-Volatile Memory Cells Characterization
body:
The trend of memory research is to develop a new memory, Non-Volatile RAM, that joins the speed of RAM with the data retention of mass memory. There are many proposals for new cell types—FeRAM, ReRAM, MRAM, STT-MRAM, and PCM among them—each based on changing the conductivity of a material using a different physical principle. This application note describes how to test an STT-MRAM cell using a pulse generator.

MRAM Technology

MRAM memory cells use Magnetic Tunnel Junctions (MTJ) consisting of two ferromagnets separated by a thin insulator. If the magnetic fields of the two ferromagnets are oriented in the same direction, electrons can tunnel from one ferromagnet to the other through the insulator layer. The first ferromagnet has a fixed magnetic field, while the field of the second can be changed by applying a current pulse to invert its orientation, changing the conductivity of the stack.

To program or erase a bit, a current pulse is applied through the stack, and the resulting magnetic field orientation depends on the current pulse direction. The efficiency of the program-and-erase process depends on the duration and amplitude of the pulse, so it can be useful during research and development to test different combinations of pulse width and amplitude using a pulse generator that lets the user change width, amplitude, and repetition rate.

Phase Change Memory (PCM)

A PCM memory cell is based on the amorphous-to-crystalline phase change of a chalcogenide material. In the amorphous phase resistance is high, and in the crystalline phase resistance is lower. To program or erase a bit, the material’s phase must be changed: a large but low voltage pulse changes the phase from amorphous to crystalline, while a short but higher voltage pulse changes it from crystalline to amorphous—so control of pulse amplitude and width is fundamental.

The Model 765 pulse generator offers a time resolution of 10 ps and a vertical resolution of 10 mV. Newer non-volatile RAM technologies require faster pulses every year, and the Model 765—with transition times under 70 ps and amplitude up to 5 Vpp—is well suited to such requirements.

MOSFET Test

In developing modern MOSFET transistors, using high-k material for the dielectric in the MOS capacitor reduces leakage current through the isolator, but causes problems from charge trapping—voltage threshold instability, carrier channel mobility degradation, and reduced reliability. Charge trapping occurs when the transistor is in the “on” state and channel charge accumulates in an isolation layer, creating a built-in potential that changes the threshold. The degree of this effect depends on the gate stack’s thickness, dielectric type, and process technology, as well as gate voltage and pulse duty cycle, so understanding the charge trapping mechanism is important to improving the technology.

Because the timescale of this effect ranges from under 1 µs to dozens of milliseconds, DC measurements are unreliable, and different types of pulsed I-V measurements are used instead, generally falling into three categories: DC Id-Vg curves (unreliable for fast-switching devices, since results depend on charge trapping from the DC bias itself), short pulse Id-Vg curves (fast-edged, nanosecond-scale pulses that reveal an intrinsic device response before charge has time to accumulate, but give no information about the trapping phenomenon itself), and slow pulse Id-Vg curves (longer, ramped-edge pulses representative of the true Id-Vg curve, since the charge doesn’t have time to accumulate if the ramp is fast enough).

The slow pulse technique can measure drain current degradation over time to observe the trapping charge effect directly, and can also be used to predict the lifetime of switching devices by studying how charge trapping effects increase before and after switching stress. The Model 765’s fast edges, wide amplitude range, adjustable baseline offset, and pulse widths from 300 ps to 1 s make it well suited to generating the pulses needed for both short and slow pulse MOSFET characterization.

title: January 27, 2025 – Laser Driver Wire Inductance
body:
This script is authored by BNC electrical engineer Cameron Simmons, excerpted from a video demonstration.

We recently began testing transistors for a new laser driver board. During the prototyping stage something came up that seemed worth sharing.

We were testing a new MOSFET on an existing driver board, and the footprint did not line up with the chip’s pins, so we needed some kind of conductive material to connect the pins to the footprint. The obvious choice was wires similar in size to the pins.

We were getting extremely low rise times with lots of ringing and distortion, despite the MOSFET being faster than the original—clearly not going to meet the specs we needed. Something in the setup was slowing the signal down. Swapping the wires for copper tape completely fixed the problem.

The issue was the self-inductance of the wires. Comparing the self-inductance of the two methods with online calculators produced a surprising result: to match the copper tape with stranded wire, we would have needed 4 AWG cable—not remotely practical. This is a good illustration of why standard wire is a poor choice for attaching a laser diode to a driver, and why we recommend our stripline cables and output PCBs instead. A wide, flat cable facilitates a clean, fast pulse even at longer distances.
